#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Render a page at 1440x900, 768x1024 and 390x844. Every backend writes the same files:
# <width>-top.png (first screen) and <width>.png (full page).
# Exits 0 on success, 1 if a capture looks blank, 3 with an "unavailable: ..." line if nothing can render.
set -uo pipefail
if [[ $# -ne 2 ]]; then echo "usage: render.sh <url-or-file> <out-dir>" >&2; exit 2; fi
target="$1"
output="$2"

## Product interpretation
- Audience, category, business model, brand constraints: backend engineers and API platform teams use it, the team lead approves the paid plan; a GitHub App that checks staging responses against an OpenAPI spec on pull requests; free for public repositories, $19 a month per private repository; no existing brand, no customers or usage numbers to show.
- Promise (who / what changes / how): backend teams with an OpenAPI spec / learn about a broken response on the pull request instead of from a client team's bug report / a GitHub App runs the spec against staging on every PR and fails the check on a mismatch.
- Five-second line, quoted as shown in the first screen (who + what): "Contractcheck is a GitHub App for backend teams. On every pull request it runs your OpenAPI spec against your staging API, and fails the check when a response stops matching the spec."
- Current alternative, including doing nothing: doing nothing and hearing it from a client team's bug report; a hand-maintained Postman collection nobody runs.
- The one advantage only this product has: it runs on every pull request by itself against staging, so a response that drifts from the spec fails the PR before merge (the Postman collection only works when someone runs it).
- Category frame (existing, subcategory or new) and what it costs to teach: existing frame "GitHub App" plus "OpenAPI spec check"; costs nothing to teach to the audience.
- Best-fit customer, and who it is not for: teams that keep an OpenAPI spec in the repo and have a staging API; not for teams without a spec, without staging, or wanting production monitoring.
- Users' own words (three phrases with source, or 'none yet'): none yet (no customers or interviews supplied); the hero adapts the trade's own validator phrasing ("expected number, got string").
- Biggest reason not to click, and the line that answers it: cost and data access; "Free for public repositories; $19 a month per private repository. It reads responses from your staging API only, never production." sits under the button.
- Conversion action and destination: "Install the GitHub App" to https://github.com/apps/contractcheck; secondary "Read the docs" to https://contractcheck.example/docs.

**Home page:** /home/claude/r8/work/W007/index.html

**What the page is:**
- **First screen.** The headline is "Expected number. Got string." Under it, one line says plainly what the product is: a GitHub App for backend teams that runs your OpenAPI spec against staging on every pull request and fails the check when a response stops matching. Then come the "Install the GitHub App" button (https://github.com/apps/contractcheck), a "Read the docs" link (https://contractcheck.example/docs), and one line on price and access: free for public repos, $19 a month per private repo, reads staging only.
- **Sample failing check.** This sits beside the headline on desktop and right under it on a phone, as the brief asks. It is a printed-style report stamped FAILED, labelled as a sample, with the three problems the brief names:
  - `currency` is missing from a response.
  - `total` was sent as the string "42.50" instead of a number.
  - The cancel endpoint returned a 409 the spec doesn't list.
- **The sample works locally.** Each problem has a fix/undo button, and the stamp turns to PASSED once all three are fixed. The response body can be edited and is re-checked as you type, with sensible messages for an empty body or invalid JSON. Reset restores the sample.
- **Sections below:**
  - Where the break gets found today (a client team's bug report) versus at the pull request.
  - Setup as one ruled form, including an example config file.
  - What it reads: staging, never production.
  - Pricing with a cost calculator for the team lead.
  - A closing call to action and a footer.

**Not on the page, because the brief doesn't supply them:** no testimonials, numbers, email addresses or sign-up form.

**Verification:**
- I rendered it at 1440, 768 and 390 wide and looked at every screenshot.
- I operated the sample through all its states at 1440 and 390, the 390 run with reduced motion, and ran the stress probes: empty input, nonsense, 5,000 characters, double clicks, reset, keyboard only, and my own JSON. All passed.
- Fixed along the way:
  - Text contrast on one section.
  - Sideways scrolling on narrow phones.
  - A font error when opening from disk.
  - The page jumping while fonts loaded.
  - A double click that could miss its button.
- Required restructure: I rebuilt the setup section, which had looked like a stock "steps beside a code block" layout.

**For the client to confirm:**
- **Config file.** The `.github/contractcheck.yml` file and its keys `spec` and `staging_url` are my guess at the shape. The page labels them as an example and points to the docs.
